level-1.title: What a bank does with your money
summary: A bank is a safe place to keep money. Safer than a pocket, a box, or under a bed.
Money in a pocket can be lost or taken. Money in a bank cannot.
The bank writes down every rupee that is yours. That written record is your account.
You can put money in and take money out when you need it. It stays yours the whole time.
The bank pays you a small extra amount for keeping your money there. A box pays you nothing.

image.alt: A bank building with a strong door

options.label: In a bank account
Loose in a school bag
Under a bed

questions.hint: Which one keeps a written record of every rupee?

questions.prompt: You put ₹100 into the bank. Whose money is it now?

image.alt: A hand placing money at a bank counter

options.label: Still yours. You can take it back.
The bank's money now

questions.hint: The bank looks after it for you. It does not keep it.

questions.prompt: ₹100 in a box for a year, or ₹100 in a bank for a year. Which is bigger at the end?

image.alt: A box beside a bank, with a small plant growing from the bank

options.label: The bank one. It pays a little extra.
The box one
Exactly the same

questions.hint: A box pays you nothing at all.

level-2.title: Opening an account in your own name
summary: You can hold a bank account in your own name from the age of 10. An adult helps manage it until you are 18, but the account is yours.
A basic account needs no minimum balance. You can open it with nothing in it, and leaving it empty costs you nothing.
It comes with a debit card, so you can pay and withdraw without asking anyone for permission.
The account is where your own money lives — pocket money, gifts, and anything you earn later.
Check the exact rules at the bank before you go. Schemes change, and different banks ask for different papers.

questions.prompt: How old must you be to hold a bank account in your own name?

image.alt: A calendar with a birthday marked

questions.hint: An adult manages it with you until 18, but your name is on it well before that.

questions.prompt: A basic account sits at ₹0 for three months. What happens?

options.label: Nothing. A basic account has no minimum balance.
The bank charges a fine
The account closes at once

questions.hint: That is the whole point of a basic account.

questions.prompt: Why have your own account instead of using a relative's?

image.alt: A single name written on an account card

options.label: The money is recorded as yours, and you control it
The bank gives you a present
It looks better

questions.hint: Think about who is allowed to take money out of an account in someone else's name.

level-3.title: The account as a foundation, and your right to one
summary: The account is not the goal. It is what everything else plugs into — a salary, a scholarship, a pension, a fund held in your name.
Money you are owed is normally paid only into an account in your own name. Without one, somebody else receives it on your behalf.
That is the real argument for holding your own: it is the difference between managing your money and being managed.
A savings account pays roughly 4% a year while prices rise around 6%. Money parked there quietly loses ground — an account is for safety and access, not for growth.
The law is behind you when you open one. The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 requires service providers, banks included, to make their services accessible.
A bank that refuses you, or insists a hearing relative speaks for you, is not following the rules. Ask for the branch manager, then the bank's grievance officer, then the RBI ombudsman.

questions.prompt: A savings account pays 4%. Prices rise 6%. What is really happening to money left in it?

image.alt: Two arrows, one rising faster than the other

options.label: It is slowly losing buying power, by about 2% a year
It is growing nicely at 4% a year
It is exactly keeping up with prices

questions.hint: Compare the two rates. Which one is larger?

questions.prompt: A clerk says you cannot open an account because you are Deaf and cannot speak to them. What is true?

image.alt: A law book beside a bank counter

options.label: They are breaking the law. Banks must make services accessible.
They are right. You need a hearing relative.
It depends on the branch

questions.hint: The RPwD Act, 2016 puts the duty on the bank, not on you.

questions.prompt: Why does the account come before any scheme or fund?

image.alt: An account at the centre with arrows leading into it

options.label: Money owed to you can only be paid into an account in your name
Banks give better rates to fund holders
You cannot take a job without one

questions.hint: Think about where a scholarship, or money taken out of a fund, actually lands.
